title: "Appendix 3 - How much do errors in the assumed prevalence change the decision curve?"
date: last-modified
---

```{r setup}
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center", dpi = 150)
suppressPackageStartupMessages({library(data.table); library(ggplot2)})
HERE <- ".." # this .qmd lives in manuscript/; repo root is ..
for (f in list.files(file.path(HERE, "R"), "^fn_.*\\.R$", full.names = TRUE)) source(f)
```

**Situation.** Every decision curve is anchored to an estimate of the taxon's landscape prevalence $\pi$.
However, the true prevalence is unknown; and expected to higher inthe AOA than across the whole domain. 
Hence, the user chosen prevalence might affect the estimated net benefit from the DCA curve. 
Here we determine the affect the accuracy of the prevalence estimate has on DCA curves. 

**Experiment.** Using the per-point method, we recompute the decision curve for the example model across a plausible prevalence band in each context: **1–5% across the whole domain** and **2–10% within the AOA**. 
For each context we swept $\pi$ across its band and recorded, at every threshold, the envelope of net benefit the SDM delivers and the envelope of the survey-all reference. 
The width of each envelope is the sensitivity of the curve to the prevalence assumption; whether the SDM envelope stays above both references is whether the *decision* is sensitive to it.

```{r prevalence-sensitivity}
#| include: false
EX <- "1arc-Iteration1-PA1:30DO:0-Seed5101" # same example model as Appendices 1-2
PT <- seq(0.001, 0.25, by = 0.002) # decision-relevant threshold range

p <- fread(file.path(HERE, "data", "holdout_point_predictions.csv"))[calibration == "raw" & design == "spatial_mapping"]
a <- fread(file.path(HERE, "data", "holdout_point_aoa.csv"))
m <- merge(p, a[, .(model, point_id, DI, DI_thresh)], by = c("model", "point_id")); m[, extrap := DI > DI_thresh]
e   <- m[model == EX] # whole domain (naive, full hold-out)
ind <- e[extrap == FALSE] # within AOA (in-domain points only)

## Net-benefit envelope of the SDM (and of survey-all) as pi sweeps a prevalence band.
band <- function(truth, prob, lo, hi, dom) {
  prevs <- seq(lo, hi, length.out = 21); mid <- (lo + hi) / 2
  M  <- sapply(prevs, function(pi) nb_exact(truth, prob, pi, PT))   # one SDM curve per prevalence
  TA <- sapply(prevs, function(pi) nb_treat_all(pi, PT))
  data.table(domain = dom, lo = lo, hi = hi, pt = PT,
             sdm_lo = apply(M, 1, min),  sdm_hi = apply(M, 1, max),  sdm_mid = nb_exact(truth, prob, mid, PT),
             ta_lo  = apply(TA, 1, min), ta_hi  = apply(TA, 1, max), ta_mid  = nb_treat_all(mid, PT))
}
DW <- "Whole domain  (prevalence 1-5%)"; DA <- "Within AOA  (prevalence 2-10%)"
df <- rbind(band(e$Presence, e$prob, 0.01, 0.05, DW),
            band(ind$Presence, ind$prob, 0.02, 0.10, DA))
df[, domain := factor(domain, levels = c(DW, DA))]
fwrite(df, file.path(HERE, "data", "prevalence_sensitivity_envelope.csv"))

## Numbers for the prose: at the "survey 5 to find 1" threshold (p_t = 0.20), how wide is the band,
## and does the SDM envelope ever fall to or below the survey-none (0) / survey-all references?
PT_MARK <- 0.20
at_mark <- df[which.min(abs(pt - PT_MARK)), .(domain, sdm_lo, sdm_hi, ta_hi)]
w_lo <- df[domain == DW & sdm_lo < 0]; a_lo <- df[domain == DA & sdm_lo < 0]
whole_width <- 100 * at_mark[domain == DW, sdm_hi - sdm_lo]
aoa_width   <- 100 * at_mark[domain == DA, sdm_hi - sdm_lo]
whole_robust <- nrow(w_lo) == 0                      # SDM lower edge stays > 0 everywhere in domain?
aoa_cross_pt <- if (nrow(a_lo)) 100 * min(a_lo$pt) else NA_real_  # first pt where AOA SDM edge dips < 0

p_prev <- ggplot(df, aes(pt)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = cda_cols[["treat_none"]], linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = PT_MARK, colour = "grey55", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = ta_lo,  ymax = ta_hi,  fill = "Survey all (treat-all)"), alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = sdm_lo, ymax = sdm_hi, fill = "SDM (per-point)"),        alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ta_mid,  colour = "Survey all (treat-all)"), linewidth = 0.5, linetype = "12") +
  geom_line(aes(y = sdm_mid, colour = "SDM (per-point)"),        linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~domain) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("SDM (per-point)" = cda_cols[["naive"]], "Survey all (treat-all)" = cda_cols[["treat_all"]]), name = NULL) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("SDM (per-point)" = cda_cols[["naive"]], "Survey all (treat-all)" = cda_cols[["treat_all"]]), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.02, 0.11)) +            # focus on the decision region; clip the deep negative tails
  labs(x = expression("Threshold probability  " * p[t]), y = "Net benefit",
       title = "Decision-curve sensitivity to the assumed landscape prevalence",
       subtitle = "Band = net benefit as the prevalence sweeps its range; line = band midpoint") +
  theme_cda()
ggsave(file.path(HERE, "figures", "dca_prevalence_sensitivity.png"), p_prev, width = 9, height = 5, dpi = 150)
```

**Result.** The two contexts have different sensitivity to prevalence uncertainty. 
Across the whole domain the SDM envelope is narrow and sits entirely above both references through the whole decision-relevant range — at the "survey five to find one" threshold it spans only about `r sprintf("%.1f", whole_width)` percentage points of net benefit and never drops to the survey-none line. 
The *decision* is robust: anywhere in the 1–5% band the model is worth using. 

Within the AOA the same sweep produces a much wider envelope (about `r sprintf("%.1f", aoa_width)` points at the same threshold). 
At the optimistic (10%) end of the band the in-domain curve keeps clear benefit through the relevant thresholds, but at the pessimistic (2%) end its lower edge drops below survey-none almost immediately`r if (!is.na(aoa_cross_pt)) sprintf(" (p_t ≈ %.0f%%)", aoa_cross_pt) else ""`. 
The in-domain comparison retains only the hard absences, and net benefit scales with how much there is to find, so the curve is far more exposed to the prevalence estimate.

```{r}
#| label: fig-prevalence-sensitivity
#| fig-cap: "Decision curves for the example model recomputed per-point across a plausible prevalence band. Each band is the net-benefit envelope as the assumed prevalence sweeps its range. The whole-domain curve is narrow and stays above both references, so the decision is insensitive to the prevalence estimate; the in-domain curve is wide and can cross the references."
p_prev
```

## A fixed-fraction view: a central estimate that is off by a set amount

The band above shows what happens across a wide range of plausible prevalences. 
A practitioner usually has a single working estimate and a worry of a different shape: *my estimate is probably in the right neighbourhood, but it could be off by a quarter, a half, three-quarters.* 
A manager who records 3% in the AOA when the truth is 6% has not used an implausible value, just one that is 50% low. 
Here we fix a central true prevalence in each context (3% whole domain, 6% within AOA) and redraw the curve as the submitted estimate departs from it by ±25%, ±50% and ±75%.

```{r misspecification}
#| include: false
## Same per-point machinery; now the prevalence is a central TRUTH misspecified by a fixed fraction.
## Note the ACTION at a given p_t (survey every unit above it) does not depend on pi -- only the net
## benefit you compute does. So this fan is the error in the *expected* benefit, and in whether the
## model still looks worthwhile, induced by a wrong prevalence; it is not a change in what is surveyed.
ERR  <- c(-0.75, -0.5, -0.25, 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75)
TRUE_W <- 0.03; TRUE_A <- 0.06 # central true prevalence per context

fan <- function(truth, prob, true_pi, dom) rbindlist(lapply(ERR, function(er)
  data.table(domain = dom, true_pi = true_pi, err = er, assumed = true_pi * (1 + er),
             pt = PT, nb = nb_exact(truth, prob, true_pi * (1 + er), PT))))
FW <- "Whole domain  (true prevalence 3%)"; FA <- "Within AOA  (true prevalence 6%)"
fx <- rbind(fan(e$Presence, e$prob, TRUE_W, FW), fan(ind$Presence, ind$prob, TRUE_A, FA))
fx[, domain := factor(domain, levels = c(FW, FA))]
fx[, errlab := factor(sprintf("%+.0f%%", 100 * err), levels = sprintf("%+.0f%%", 100 * ERR))]
fwrite(fx, file.path(HERE, "data", "prevalence_misspecification_fan.csv"))

## Survey-all reference, drawn once at each context's TRUE prevalence: the benchmark the SDM must beat.
## The vertical gap from a (mis)specified SDM curve down to this line is the model's benefit over
## surveying everything, so a wrong prevalence is seen shrinking or inflating that gap.
ref <- rbind(data.table(domain = FW, pt = PT, nb = nb_treat_all(TRUE_W, PT)),
             data.table(domain = FA, pt = PT, nb = nb_treat_all(TRUE_A, PT)))
ref[, domain := factor(domain, levels = c(FW, FA))]

## Prose numbers: whole domain stays beneficial even at the worst underestimate; within the AOA the
## break-even threshold (where the drawn SDM curve crosses survey-none) moves a lot with the estimate.
cross0 <- function(dt) { i <- which(dt$nb < 0)[1]; if (is.na(i)) NA_real_ else 100 * dt$pt[i] }
whole_worst_pos <- fx[domain == FW & err == -0.75, all(nb > 0)]       # model still beats survey-none?
a_true <- cross0(fx[domain == FA & err == 0]); a_lo <- cross0(fx[domain == FA & err == -0.5]); a_hi <- cross0(fx[domain == FA & err == 0.5])

pal <- setNames(colorRampPalette(c(cda_cols[["aoa"]], "grey80", cda_cols[["treat_all"]]))(length(ERR)),
                sprintf("%+.0f%%", 100 * ERR))
pal["+0%"] <- cda_cols[["treat_none"]]              # the true curve, drawn dark and heavy
p_mis <- ggplot(fx, aes(pt, nb, colour = errlab)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = cda_cols[["treat_none"]], linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = PT_MARK, colour = "grey55", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line(data = ref, aes(pt, nb, linetype = "Survey all"),
            colour = cda_cols[["treat_all"]], linewidth = 0.7, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_line(data = fx[err != 0], linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_line(data = fx[err == 0], linewidth = 1.1) +
  facet_wrap(~domain) +
  scale_colour_manual(name = "Prevalence estimate error", values = pal,
                      guide = guide_legend(nrow = 2, order = 1)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(name = NULL, values = c("Survey all" = "dashed"),
                        guide = guide_legend(order = 2, override.aes = list(colour = cda_cols[["treat_all"]]))) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.02, 0.085)) +
  labs(x = expression("Threshold probability  " * p[t]), y = "Net benefit",
       title = "Decision curve drawn with a misspecified prevalence") +
  theme_cda()
ggsave(file.path(HERE, "figures", "dca_prevalence_misspecification.png"), p_mis, width = 9, height = 5, dpi = 150)
```

Because the per-point action at a threshold does not depend on prevalence, misspecifying it does not change *which* sites you survey; it only distorts the net benefit you should anticipate. 
This distortion is small where there is little to find and large where there is more: across the whole domain even a 75%-low estimate keeps the curve `r if (whole_worst_pos) "above survey-none throughout" else "near, but occasionally below, survey-none"`, so the model stays clearly worthwhile. 
Within the AOA the break-even threshold, where the drawn curve meets survey-none, moves from about `r sprintf("%.0f%%", a_true)` at the true 6% to roughly `r sprintf("%.0f%%", a_lo)` if the estimate is 50% low and `r sprintf("%.0f%%", a_hi)` if it is 50% high, so a modest error slides the apparent range of useful thresholds up or down by a meaningful margin.

```{r}
#| label: fig-prevalence-misspecification
#| fig-cap: "The same example model, now with a single central true prevalence (3% whole domain, 6% within AOA) misspecified by a fixed fraction. The heavy dark line is the truth; warmer curves overestimate, cooler curves underestimate. The dashed line is survey-all at the true prevalence. Across the whole domain the curve is well above both references even at a 75%-low estimate. While within the AOA the same fractional error swings the gap, and the break-even threshold, substantially, because net benefit there is far more sensitive to prevalence."
p_mis
```

**Conclusion.** It is worth buffering occurence points, to estimate the prevalence, and to calculate the area of AOA, using a GIS, to refine estimates. 
Where the curve stays clear of the survey-all and survey-none references, as across the whole domain here, both a wide plausible range and a sizeable error in a central estimate leave the recommendation intact. 
Within the AOA, whose narrower, harder comparison makes net benefit scale steeply with prevalence, the same uncertainty moves the break-even threshold enough to change the advice; pin the prevalence down before trusting the curve at selective thresholds. 
In every case the prevalence estimate changes the net benefit you *expect*, not the sites the model tells you to survey at a given threshold.
